lesson.title: Inside the IPv4 Header: Twenty Bytes That Route the Entire Internet
lesson.summary: The IPv4 header is a 20 to 60 byte structure that precedes every packet's payload, packing version, length, fragmentation, time to live, protocol, checksum, and address fields into a format every router on the internet reads.
lesson.body:
Every IPv4 packet begins with a structured header that a router reads before it looks at anything else, and that header is what actually carries out the addressing and control that IPv4 as a protocol promises. The header has a minimum size of 20 bytes and can extend up to 60 bytes when optional fields are present, and every field in it exists to answer one specific question a router or a receiving host needs answered quickly, since routers process this header for every packet that passes through them.

The first byte splits into two 4 bit fields: Version, which is always set to 4 for IPv4, and IHL, the Internet Header Length, which records the header's total length in 32 bit words rather than bytes. Because IHL is only 4 bits wide, it can express a maximum value of 15, and 15 words of 4 bytes each is exactly 60 bytes, the header's hard ceiling; the minimum legal value of 5 words gives the standard 20 byte header with no options. Next comes an 8 bit Type of Service field, now generally used for differentiated services and explicit congestion notification, followed by a 16 bit Total Length field that records the size of the entire packet, header plus payload, capping any single IPv4 packet at 65,535 bytes.

Three fields work together to handle fragmentation, the process of splitting a packet that is too large for a given link into smaller pieces: a 16 bit Identification field lets a receiver group fragments that belong to the same original packet, a set of Flags including the Do not Fragment (DF) and More Fragments (MF) bits controls whether fragmentation is even allowed and whether more fragments are still coming, and a 13 bit Fragment Offset records where each fragment fits back into the original packet. An 8 bit Time to Live (TTL) field is decremented by one at every router hop and forces the packet to be discarded once it hits zero, which is what prevents a misrouted packet from circulating the internet forever, and an 8 bit Protocol field identifies what kind of payload follows, such as the value 6 for TCP, 17 for UDP, or 1 for ICMP.

The remaining fixed fields are a 16 bit Header Checksum, a validation over the header alone, not the payload, and recalculated at every hop since TTL changes each time, followed by the two fields the whole packet exists to deliver: a 32 bit Source Address and a 32 bit Destination Address, each written in the dotted decimal address format used everywhere IPv4 addresses appear. Any bytes beyond the mandatory 20 make up the Options field, used for less common features like source routing or timestamping, padded out so the header always ends on a 32 bit boundary; because options are rare in ordinary traffic, most IPv4 packets in practice carry exactly the minimum 20 byte header.

Every field here earns its place by keeping routers fast: a router forwarding millions of packets per second only ever needs to read the Destination Address to make its next hop decision, decrement TTL by one, and recompute the checksum, which is why the header keeps the fields a router touches on every packet fixed, small, and near the front, while the rarely used Options field is pushed to the end where it costs nothing when absent.
